script.title: The Con Man Who Sold the Eiffel Tower for Scrap
sentences: In 1925, a con man sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap.
Victor Lustig had read in a Paris newspaper that the tower was costly to maintain.
He had a forger make fake government stationery.
Posing as a government official, he met scrap metal dealers at an expensive hotel.
He said the government wished to sell the tower secretly, to avoid public outcry.
Dealer André Poisson paid a large bribe plus around 70,000 francs, and Lustig fled to Austria.
No newspaper ever mentioned the con.
So he went back to Paris and found a second buyer for the same tower.
scenes: Extreme close-up of con man Victor Lustig's face, 1925, sly triumphant smile, one eyebrow raised, thin moustache, fedora brim shadowing his eyes, the Eiffel Tower blurred behind him in golden Paris dusk light.

Victor Lustig in a 1920s three-piece suit at a Paris cafe table, frowning thoughtfully over an open newspaper, coffee cup beside him, the Eiffel Tower visible through the window, soft morning light, medium shot.

A 1920s Paris back-room workshop: a hunched forger with spectacles carefully pressing an official-looking seal onto blank cream paper while Victor Lustig watches with a satisfied smirk, warm lamplight, over-the-shoulder shot.

Victor Lustig posing as a stern government official in a dark suit, addressing five attentive scrap metal dealers around a polished table in a lavish 1920s Paris hotel suite, chandeliers glowing, wide shot.
Victor Lustig leaning forward, finger to his lips in a conspiratorial gesture, the dealers' faces tense and intrigued, heavy velvet curtains drawn, low amber light, close medium shot.

Eager scrap dealer André Poisson in a 1920s suit handing a thick envelope across a hotel table to Victor Lustig, who smiles coolly; behind, a train window at night hints at escape, warm and cold light contrast.
Victor Lustig in a 1920s Vienna cafe anxiously flipping through a stack of French newspapers, then relaxing with a puzzled grin, winter light through the window, medium close-up.
Victor Lustig stepping off a steam train onto a Paris platform, hat tipped, confident grin, the Eiffel Tower rising in the misty distance, morning light, low-angle wide shot.
script.description:
In 1925, Victor Lustig sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap.
Then he came back to sell it again.
claims_en: In 1925 Victor Lustig, a con artist, sold the Eiffel Tower to a scrap metal dealer in a scam.
In Paris he read a newspaper article about the problems of maintaining the Eiffel Tower; the city found it increasingly expensive to maintain and repaint.
He hired a forger to produce fake government stationery.
He invited scrap metal dealers to a confidential meeting at an expensive hotel, posing as a government official (Deputy Director-General of the Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs).
He told them the French government wished to sell the tower for scrap, and that nothing could be disclosed because the deal would likely spark public outcry.
André Poisson paid a large bribe and the funds for the sale, around 70,000 francs.
He could find no reference to the con in newspapers, so he returned to Paris to pull off the scheme again.
On the second attempt he found another mark willing to buy the Eiffel Tower.
